Quick follow-up: our engineering leadership wants a concise recommendation we can take to procurement — specifically comparing a fully private (VPC/on-prem air-gapped) deployment versus Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pool) for our regulated inference workloads.

Things that matter to us:
- Predictable latency under 99th percentile constraints
- Data residency and auditability (we need detailed logs for quarterly audits)
- Cost sensitivity for bursty traffic patterns (we have weekly spikes tied to batch jobs)
- Contract timing — procurement needs lead times for hardware/commitments

Attached is a small traffic sample (not included here) and our compliance checklist. Can you share: 1) a short tradeoff table, 2) a recommended fleet split if we wanted to use both reserved and burst capacity, and 3) what evidence/artefacts Redwood can provide for SOC2 / access logs?

Appreciate a one-page summary we can hand to procurement by Friday.

Best,

Hi Elaine — thanks for the clear ask. High level first, then we'll follow up with a short one-pager and a cost model (attached).

Short tradeoff summary (private vs dedicated):
- Private (VPC/on-prem):
  - Pros: full network isolation, customer-managed KMS, easiest path for strict air-gap/regulatory controls.
  - Cons: higher TCO, longer procurement/onboarding (hardware + install windows), Redwood support model is via onsite/remote ops package.
- Dedicated (reserved pool):
  - Pros: predictable per-token economics at committed levels, faster time to production, Redwood handles runtime ops and kernel optimizations.
  - Cons: requires contractual SLAs for data handling and may need additional evidence for some auditors (we can provide logs & KMS integration, but not physical air-gaps).

Recommended initial fleet approach for your traffic pattern: hybrid reserved + burst:
- Commit to ~70–80% of projected steady-state GPU capacity in Dedicated (reserved). This secures price and predictable latency.
- Keep 20–30% of expected peak as burstable capacity (hosted or short-term reserved) for weekly spikes.
- For the strictest workloads (PHI-heavy flows), use Private deployment for that partition only, and route lower-risk traffic to Dedicated.

I've attached a conservative fleet_cost_model.xlsx with a 12-month cost comparison and a private-deploy-checklist.pdf that lists items procurement will ask for.

Rishi — adding some notes on perf/cold-start and batch sizing below. Jonas — can you confirm procurement path and suggested contract vehicles (commit bands, term lengths)?

I'll produce the one-page summary by EOD tomorrow.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park

Adding technical detail so procurement/engineering have realistic expectations. Key points:

1) Latency stability and 99th pctn
- Dedicated reserved capacity gives us the ability to pin model shards and prewarm KV caches; 99th percentile latency is far easier to guarantee if you have reserved GPUs sized for peak QPS.

2) Burst handling patterns
- We can support burst capacity in two ways: (a) short-term hosted burst (elastic capacity in same region) or (b) short-duration reserved burst (pre-provisioned but paid at a higher burst rate). Hosted burst offers fastest activation but slightly higher per-token cost.

3) Cold-start / cache warm-up
- For large context models, cold starts add ~50–150ms per request depending on sequence length. For predictable 99th pctn, keep a small warm pool of pods (2–4 GPUs) dedicated to critical routes.

4) Quantization and model variants
- Use an int8 variant on Dedicated for predictable perf/cost. For Private, we can still run quantized models but verify bit-exactness against your QA set; R&D will run a quick eval if you want.

5) Audit/logging evidence
- We can provide: request-level access logs (timestamped), encryption-at-rest and in-transit summaries, key rotation logs (KMS integration), and SOC2 summary package. For Private, we can include network diagrams and deployment manifests for auditors.

Operational recommendation (short):
- Reserved Dedicated for baseline and critical routes (70–80%).
- Hosted burst for spiky, non-PHI traffic (20%).
- Private batch for PHI-heavy pipelines and quarterly audit windows.

Rishi

Hi Elaine — looping in procurement path and an initial commercial construct.

Commercial recommendation:
- Term: 12-months initial commitment with quarterly usage reviews.
- Commit band: cover 75% of forecast steady-state (we can model 60/75/90% tiers in the attached workbook).
- Burst: 20–25% available as on-demand host capacity billed at a premium; option to convert burst usage into committed capacity at the next quarter with pro-rated credits.
- Private deployments (air-gapped) are priced as a separate SOW: includes a one-time on-boarding fee + monthly platform license + optional on-call SLA.

Suggested procurement milestones:
1) Get NDA executed (if not already).
2) Exchange SOC2 evidence pack and Private checklist (we attached SOC2_evidence_summary.pdf).
3) Sign term-sheet (DocuSign link below) for reserved capacity band.
4) Schedule 4-week onboarding window for Dedicated; 8–12 week for Private on-prem.

DocuSign: https://app.docusign.com/doc/ABC123

If you prefer, we can frame this as a hybrid order: Dedicated reserve for all inference with a carve-out to run PHI in a Private VPC for the first 90 days while your auditors review. That reduces initial on-prem scope but preserves compliance controls.
